features_intro: The revised program of Master of Science in Computer Science (MSCS) contains several features and characteristics relevant to the current trends and standards.
feature_1: The revised program is an academic track and has a total of 34 units.
feature_2: Revising the core courses into four (4) theory courses with a total of twelve (12) units, in compliance with CMO No. 7, series of 2010
feature_3: Addition of new requirement for comprehensive examination required under CMO No. 15, series of 2019
feature_4: Addition of new requirement for special common course for the mainstreaming of peace and development
feature_5: Addition of new requirement for systematic literature review and seminar leading to research capability development
feature_6: Addition of new and relevant specialization courses under theory and systems category
feature_7: Compliance with the Outcomes-based QA in higher education as prescribed by Commission on Higher Education (CHED)
feature_8: Use of the new prefix CSC in all of its courses
feature_9: Compliance with the standard course coding of the Institute
rationale:
The field of computing is dynamic and has developed into mature and independent discipline as Computer Science. The timely and rapid developments in computing technology such as artificial intelligence, data mining, data communications, and security anchored on the theories and principles of computing continue to enrich the discipline.

The Department of Computer Science, in order to rectify perceived deficiencies in the old program and to maintain its relevance and currency, advance this revision. The impact of this rapidly evolving discipline where its technology contributions become part of everyday life of the people will require the new program to adjust its graduate curriculum for the new attributes and competencies required in this modern digital era.

In view of the guidelines of the CHED prescribing the criteria and standards of MSCS program and the latest policies, standards and guidelines for graduate programs, the proposed revised program is an academic track with courses incorporating the latest trends in artificial intelligence and analytics. The revised program is deemed to provide the balance of theory and practice.

The Computer Science graduate curriculum is based on local, national, and international criteria and standards. This means that the graduates of the program will be adequately prepared for advanced academic pursuits, and they will be equipped with the knowledge and skills required for the Industry 4.0 implementation. The outcomes-based quality assurance is expected to address these goals through the compliance of standards set by CHED Memo 46, series 2012.

This curricular revision will mainstream the promotion of peace and development in Mindanao and beyond -- computing with its inevitable roles as a tool in shaping or aiding the socio-cultural, socio-political, and socio-economic aspects of society, its pervasiveness in government, business, industry, education, and all sectors of society in general. The ubiquity of the computing technology enabled people to communicate, collaborate, interact, and share ideas, thereby providing opportunities for unity and borderless communities and better understanding among people.
prog_obj_intro: The goal of the program administration of Computer Science is to provide excellence in Computer Science program through modern application of computing. The MSCS should always be responsive to the modern trends and aligned to the standards of the discipline and use the best recognized practices to produce reliable and successful professionals.

peo_intro: The program educational objectives (PEO) of the MSCS is to achieve the set of attributes for the alumni achievable after graduation are given below.
peo_1: Engage in the productive practice as Computer Science professional to solve complex and significant problems across broad-range of application areas.
peo_2: Adapt to technology advances and acquire new knowledge through continued professional growth and by embracing life-long learning.
peo_3: Make well-rounded and fair decisions when faced with social, ethical, legal, and environmental issues inherent to computing practices.

clos.description: Apply asymptotic analysis, recurrence relations, and amortized analysis to evaluate the time and space complexity of algorithms.
Design and implement advanced data structures including balanced search trees (AVL, Red-Black), priority queues, hash tables, and graph representations.
Apply algorithm design paradigms—divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms—to solve complex combinatorial and optimization problems.
Construct formal proofs of algorithm correctness using loop invariants, mathematical induction, and reduction techniques.
Evaluate and select appropriate algorithms and data structures for given problem constraints and real-world performance requirements.

courses.desc: Advanced study of data structures and algorithm design and analysis; abstract data types such as stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, and graphs; advanced sorting and searching; algorithm complexity and correctness.

learning_plan.topic: Review of Algorithm Analysis and Asymptotic Notation
learning_plan.llo: Review big-O, Ω, and Θ notation; apply the master theorem and substitution method to solve recurrences; analyze best, average, and worst cases.

learning_plan.topic: Advanced Sorting: Heapsort, Mergesort, Lower Bounds
learning_plan.llo: Prove Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison-based sorting; implement and analyze Heapsort and Mergesort; introduce linear-time sorting (Counting, Radix, Bucket).
Implement randomized and median-of-medians selection algorithms; apply aggregate, accounting, and potential methods for amortized analysis.

learning_plan.topic: Balanced Binary Search Trees: AVL and Red-Black Trees
learning_plan.llo: Implement AVL and Red-Black tree rotations, insertions, and deletions; prove height bounds and amortized costs.
Augment BSTs for order statistics and interval trees; design and implement B-Tree search, insert, and delete for disk-based storage.

learning_plan.topic: Hashing: Hash Tables, Universal Hashing, and Perfect Hashing
learning_plan.llo: Analyze chaining and open-addressing hash tables; implement universal hashing; describe and analyze perfect hashing for static sets.

learning_plan.topic: Dynamic Programming: Principles and Classic Problems
learning_plan.llo: Apply the principle of optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; solve rod cutting, matrix-chain multiplication, and LCS using DP.

learning_plan.topic: Dynamic Programming: Advanced Problems — Midterm Exam
learning_plan.llo: Apply DP to optimal BST, 0/1 knapsack, and edit distance; derive time/space complexity of DP solutions.
Apply the greedy-choice property and prove correctness via exchange arguments; solve activity selection, Huffman coding, and fractional knapsack.

learning_plan.topic: Graph Representations and Traversal: BFS and DFS
learning_plan.llo: Implement adjacency list and matrix representations; analyze BFS and DFS for shortest-path trees, topological sort, and SCC (Tarjan's/Kosaraju's).

learning_plan.topic: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, and Floyd-Warshall
learning_plan.llo: Implement and analyze Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue; prove Bellman-Ford correctness for negative edges; apply Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs shortest paths.
Implement Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms; prove MST correctness using the cut property; design an efficient Union-Find with path compression and union by rank.

learning_plan.topic: Network Flow: Max-Flow Min-Cut and Ford-Fulkerson
learning_plan.llo: Prove the max-flow min-cut theorem; implement Ford-Fulkerson and Edmonds-Karp algorithms; apply max-flow to bipartite matching.

learning_plan.topic: Randomized Algorithms: QuickSort Analysis and Hashing
learning_plan.llo: Apply probabilistic analysis and indicator random variables; analyze expected running time of Randomized QuickSort; design randomized data structures.
learning_plan.resources: CLRS Ch. 5, 7; MR – Randomized Algorithms Ch. 1

learning_plan.llo: Design and analyze approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems (vertex cover, TSP, set cover); relate to NP-completeness and intractability.

courses.desc: Theoretical foundations of computer science. Formal languages and automata; regular expressions, context-free languages, parsing; Turing machines and complexity; partial recursive functions; undecidability; program correctness.

clos.description: Explain the mathematical foundations underlying formal languages, automata, and the theory of computation.
Construct and analyze formal models of computation including finite automata, pushdown automata, and Turing machines.
Apply formal language theory to solve problems involving language recognition, parsing, and pattern matching.
Assess the decidability and undecidability of computational problems using formal reduction techniques.
Analyze the computational complexity of problems and classify them within the hierarchy of complexity classes (P, NP, NP-complete).

learning_plan.llo: Review sets, relations, functions, graphs, strings, and proof techniques (induction, contradiction) used throughout the course.
Define DFAs formally, trace computations, construct DFAs for given languages, and prove language membership.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 1.1; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 2

learning_plan.topic: Nondeterministic Finite Automata (NFA) and Equivalence with DFA
learning_plan.llo: Define NFAs, apply the subset construction to convert NFAs to DFAs, and demonstrate closure properties of regular languages.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 1.2; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 2

learning_plan.llo: Convert among regular expressions, DFAs, and NFAs; prove that regular expressions and finite automata describe the same class of languages.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 1.3; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 3

learning_plan.topic: Properties of Regular Languages and the Pumping Lemma
learning_plan.llo: Apply the Pumping Lemma to prove that specific languages are not regular; demonstrate closure and decision properties.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 1.4; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 4

learning_plan.llo: Define CFGs and derivations, design CFGs for given languages, convert CFGs to Chomsky Normal Form (CNF).
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 2.1; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 5

learning_plan.llo: Define PDAs formally, construct PDAs for context-free languages, and prove equivalence of CFGs and PDAs.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 2.2; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 6

learning_plan.llo: Apply the Pumping Lemma for CFLs to show non-context-freeness; describe closure and decision properties of CFLs.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 2.3; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 7

learning_plan.llo: Define Turing machines (TMs) formally, trace TM computations, and design TMs to recognize or decide languages.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 3; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 8

learning_plan.topic: Variants of Turing Machines and the Church-Turing Thesis
learning_plan.llo: Describe multi-tape TMs, nondeterministic TMs, and enumerators; articulate the Church-Turing thesis and its implications.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 3.2–3.3; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 8

learning_plan.llo: Distinguish decidable from undecidable languages; prove decidability of problems about DFAs, CFGs, and certain TM problems.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 4; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 9

learning_plan.llo: Use mapping reducibility and Rice’s theorem to prove undecidability; analyze the halting problem and its consequences.

learning_plan.topic: Complexity Theory: P, NP, and NP-Completeness
learning_plan.llo: Define time complexity classes P and NP; apply polynomial-time reductions to prove NP-completeness using Cook–Levin theorem and standard NP-complete problems.
learning_plan.resources: Sipser Ch. 7; Hopcroft et al. Ch. 10

clos.description: Explain the design of modern processor architectures including pipelining, cache hierarchies, multicore organization, and memory systems.
Analyze operating system abstractions including process and thread management, scheduling algorithms, and inter-process communication mechanisms.
Apply virtual memory management techniques including paging, segmentation, TLBs, and page replacement policies.
Evaluate file system design, I/O subsystem organization, and storage hierarchies in modern operating systems.

learning_plan.topic: Computer Organization Review; Instruction Set Architecture
learning_plan.llo: Review ISA design (CISC vs. RISC); trace instruction fetch-decode-execute cycles; compare x86 and ARM architectures.
Design a 5-stage pipeline; identify and resolve data, control, and structural hazards using forwarding, stalling, and branch prediction.

learning_plan.topic: Memory Hierarchy: Caches and Virtual Memory
learning_plan.llo: Analyze direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully-associative caches; calculate hit rates and AMAT; explain TLB operation.
Explain SMP and NUMA memory models; analyze cache coherence protocols (MSI, MESI); discuss memory consistency models.

learning_plan.topic: OS Overview: Structure, System Calls, and Processes
learning_plan.llo: Describe monolithic vs. microkernel OS structures; trace system call execution; define process state machine and PCB.

learning_plan.topic: CPU Scheduling: Algorithms and Performance Metrics
learning_plan.llo: Evaluate FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, and priority scheduling; compute turnaround time, waiting time, and CPU utilization; analyze multilevel queue scheduling.

learning_plan.topic: Synchronization: Locks, Semaphores, Monitors — Midterm Exam
learning_plan.llo: Implement mutual exclusion using Peterson's algorithm, semaphores, and monitors; solve producer-consumer and readers-writers problems.
Model deadlock using resource allocation graphs; implement Banker's algorithm; compare deadlock handling strategies.

learning_plan.topic: Virtual Memory: Paging and Page Tables
learning_plan.llo: Explain paging hardware and multi-level page tables; trace address translation with TLBs; compute effective memory access time.
Simulate FIFO, LRU, Optimal, and Clock replacement algorithms; analyze thrashing and the working-set model.
Explain file system data structures (superblock, inodes, directory entries); compare FAT, ext4, and NTFS allocation strategies.
Describe I/O hardware, polling, interrupt-driven I/O, and DMA; analyze disk scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN); compare HDD and SSD I/O models.
Trace the Linux process scheduler (CFS), memory manager, and VFS layer; analyze kernel data structures using source code excerpts.

learning_plan.topic: Emerging Architectures: GPUs, FPGAs, and Cloud Systems
learning_plan.llo: Describe GPU architecture and SIMT execution; contrast FPGA reconfigurable computing with CPU/GPU; discuss cloud hypervisor architecture.

clos.description: Explain and discuss basic concepts in computer modelling and simulation.
Apply mathematical and computational models using tools such as SciLab, NetLogo, and R to simulate real-world phenomena.
Analyze and communicate simulation results effectively using scientific writing, visualization, and presentation.

courses.desc: CSC 210 introduces the principles and practices of computer modelling and simulation used to understand, analyze, and predict complex real-world systems. Students will explore modeling concepts such as abstraction, system dynamics, input/output relationships, and verification/validation of simulation results. The course incorporates hands-on use of simulation tools such as SciLab, NetLogo, and R to design and implement computational models. Applications span across natural sciences, social behavior, and decision systems. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, scientific communication, and ethical considerations in modeling decisions.

learning_plan.llo: Describe the purpose, nature, and scope of modelling and simulation in computer science.

Develop basic mathematical models and apply simple statistical methods.

Create agent-based models to simulate social and ecological systems.
Present an initial simulation model and explain assumptions and early results.
Differentiate between verification and validation processes.
Use R to analyze datasets and run stochastic simulations.
Refine a full simulation project and prepare documentation.

courses.desc: This course explores foundational and advanced methods in computational science, including numerical modeling, algorithmic simulation, and high-performance computing for solving real-world scientific problems. Emphasis is placed on understanding the computational representations of physical systems, validation of numerical methods, and interpretation of simulation results in various domains. Topics may include numerical linear algebra, finite difference methods, Monte Carlo methods, parallel computing, and data-driven modeling using machine learning.

clos.description: Explain the fundamental concepts and operational principles of cellular automata.
Apply cellular automata to represent numbers, perform arithmetic operations, and model mathematical functions.

courses.desc: CSC 292 explores advanced theoretical constructs in computer science through the lens of cellular automata—a discrete computational model inspired by natural systems. Students investigate how simple local rules applied to grids of cells give rise to complex global behavior. The course delves into the mathematical foundations, representations, and computational capabilities of cellular automata, including their ability to simulate Turing machines. Topics include number representation, arithmetic operations, mathematical modeling, applications to real-world systems (e.g., biology, fluid dynamics, economics), and the Principle of Computational Equivalence. Emphasis is placed on both the theoretical insights and the practical implementation of cellular automata using programming tools. The course culminates in a project that demonstrates the use of cellular automata to address a problem or simulate a system.

Use Cellular Automata to represent numbers and perform arithmetic.

learning_plan.llo: Model mathematical functions and systems (e.g., chaos, PDEs) using Cellular Automata.

Explain the computational universality of Cellular Automata and apply it to solve theoretical problems.

courses.title: Cryptography

clos.description: Explain the mathematical foundations of cryptography including modular arithmetic, number theory, probability, and information theory.
Analyze classical and modern symmetric cryptographic systems including block ciphers (AES, DES) and stream ciphers.
Design and evaluate asymmetric cryptosystems including RSA, ElGamal, and elliptic curve cryptography.
Assess cryptographic hash functions, digital signature schemes, and public key infrastructure (PKI).
Apply cryptographic protocols to design secure communication systems and evaluate their security properties.

learning_plan.llo: Describe the goals of cryptography (confidentiality, integrity, authentication); survey classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, Playfair) and their weaknesses.

learning_plan.topic: Mathematical Foundations: Modular Arithmetic and Number Theory
learning_plan.llo: Apply the extended Euclidean algorithm, Chinese Remainder Theorem, Fermat's Little Theorem, and Euler's theorem to cryptographic problems.
learning_plan.resources: Stinson Appendix; Katz & Lindell Appendix A

learning_plan.topic: Shannon's Information Theory and Perfect Secrecy
learning_plan.llo: Define entropy and perfect secrecy; prove the one-time pad achieves perfect secrecy; state Shannon's impossibility theorem for perfect secrecy.
Describe the Feistel structure of DES and the SubBytes/ShiftRows/MixColumns/AddRoundKey structure of AES; analyze their security properties.

learning_plan.topic: Block Cipher Modes of Operation and Stream Ciphers
learning_plan.llo: Compare ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB, and CTR modes; implement and analyze RC4 and ChaCha20 stream ciphers; identify chosen-plaintext and chosen-ciphertext attacks.
Apply differential and linear cryptanalysis to reduced-round ciphers; assess the importance of S-box design in resistance to algebraic attacks.
learning_plan.resources: Stinson Ch. 3; Biham & Shamir – Differential Cryptanalysis

learning_plan.llo: Derive and implement RSA encryption and decryption; prove security based on integer factorization; analyze RSA-OAEP padding and common attacks.

learning_plan.topic: Midterm Exam + Discrete Logarithm and Diffie-Hellman
learning_plan.llo: Explain the discrete logarithm problem; implement Diffie-Hellman key exchange; analyze man-in-the-middle attacks and authenticated key exchange.
Implement ElGamal encryption and signature; define elliptic curve groups over finite fields; compare ECC key sizes with RSA for equivalent security.
learning_plan.resources: Stinson Ch. 6; Hankerson et al. – Guide to ECC

learning_plan.topic: Cryptographic Hash Functions: SHA and HMAC
learning_plan.llo: Define collision resistance, preimage resistance, and second-preimage resistance; analyze SHA-2 and SHA-3 construction; implement HMAC.

learning_plan.topic: Digital Signatures: RSA, DSA, and ECDSA
learning_plan.llo: Implement RSA-PSS and DSA signature schemes; analyze ECDSA used in TLS; describe signature security under chosen-message attacks.
Explain X.509 certificate structure, certificate chains, and the role of CAs; describe OCSP and CRL for certificate revocation; trace TLS handshake.
Trace Kerberos ticket-granting protocol; analyze challenge-response and zero-knowledge authentication; identify replay attack vulnerabilities.

learning_plan.topic: Secure Communication Protocols: TLS and Signal
learning_plan.llo: Trace TLS 1.3 handshake and record protocol; analyze the Signal protocol's double ratchet; evaluate forward secrecy and post-compromise security.
learning_plan.resources: Rescorla – TLS 1.3; Marlinspike & Perrin – Signal Protocol

learning_plan.llo: Describe quantum threats to RSA and ECC; survey NIST PQC standardization candidates (Kyber, Dilithium); discuss lattice-based and hash-based cryptography.
learning_plan.resources: NIST PQC Project documentation; Bernstein & Lange – Post-Quantum Cryptography

learning_plan.llo: Review TLS, IPsec, and SSH protocols from a security perspective; trace authentication and key exchange flows; identify protocol-level attacks.

learning_plan.topic: Security Policies: Formal Models and Policy Languages

learning_plan.resources: VanderPlas Ch. 4; Tukey – Exploratory Data Analysis (selected)

learning_plan.resources: Wasserman – All of Statistics Ch. 9–11; scipy.stats documentation

learning_plan.resources: James et al. – ISLR Ch. 3; sklearn linear_model documentation

learning_plan.resources: VanderPlas Ch. 5; McInnes et al. – UMAP (paper)

learning_plan.llo: Apply Tufte's data-ink ratio principle; choose appropriate chart types for different data relationships; identify misleading visualization patterns.
learning_plan.resources: Wilke – Fundamentals of Data Visualization; Tufte – The Visual Display of Quantitative Information

learning_plan.llo: Create interactive dashboards using Plotly and Dash (or Bokeh); implement brushing, linking, and drill-down interactions.
learning_plan.resources: Plotly documentation; Bokeh documentation; VanderPlas Ch. 4

learning_plan.resources: Bird et al. – NLTK Book (selected); sklearn text feature extraction

learning_plan.resources: O'Neil – Weapons of Math Destruction (selected chapters); Dwork & Roth

clos.description: Explain the theoretical foundations of programming languages including the untyped and simply-typed lambda calculus.
Analyze the formal operational and denotational semantics of programming language constructs.
Apply type systems including simple types, parametric polymorphism, subtyping, and type inference to ensure program safety.
Evaluate the design of language features—evaluation order, mutation, continuations, and modules—through semantic analysis.
Implement components of a programming language interpreter, type checker, or evaluator based on formal semantic specifications.

learning_plan.topic: Introduction: Syntax, Semantics, and Language Design
learning_plan.llo: Distinguish syntax from semantics; describe abstract syntax trees; motivate formal semantics for defining language behavior unambiguously.
learning_plan.resources: Pierce – TAPL Ch. 1; Winskel – The Formal Semantics of PLs Ch. 1

learning_plan.topic: Untyped Arithmetic Expressions: Small-Step and Big-Step Semantics
learning_plan.llo: Define small-step (structural operational) and big-step (natural) semantics for arithmetic and Boolean expressions; prove progress and preservation.

learning_plan.topic: Untyped Lambda Calculus: Syntax and Evaluation
learning_plan.llo: Define the untyped lambda calculus syntax; apply β-reduction (full, call-by-value, call-by-name); encode booleans, numbers, and pairs as lambda terms.
Represent lambda terms using de Bruijn indices; implement substitution and shifting; implement a lambda calculus evaluator.
Extend the lambda calculus with simple types; define typing rules and type derivations; prove type safety (progress + preservation) for STLC.

learning_plan.topic: Extensions to STLC: Products, Sums, and References
learning_plan.llo: Add product types, sum types, and unit to STLC; introduce mutable references and the store; analyze the effect of state on type safety.
Define equi-recursive and iso-recursive types; specify subtyping rules for records and functions; analyze the Liskov Substitution Principle formally.

learning_plan.topic: Midterm Exam + Parametric Polymorphism: System F
learning_plan.llo: Extend STLC to System F (polymorphic lambda calculus); write polymorphic type annotations; prove that System F is strongly normalizing.

learning_plan.topic: Type Inference: Hindley-Milner and Algorithm W
learning_plan.llo: Derive type inference constraints; implement Algorithm W (unification-based); explain let-polymorphism and value restriction.
Define semantic domains and continuous functions; give denotational semantics for PCF; explain fixed-point semantics for recursion.
Write Hoare triples and derive pre/post conditions; prove partial and total correctness of loops using loop invariants; apply weakest precondition calculus.
learning_plan.resources: Winskel Ch. 6–7; Dijkstra – A Discipline of Programming (selected)

learning_plan.llo: Implement call-by-need evaluation using environments and thunks; analyze lazy vs. eager evaluation trade-offs; discuss Haskell's evaluation model.
learning_plan.resources: Pierce – TAPL Ch. 11; Launchbury – A Natural Semantics for Lazy Evaluation

learning_plan.llo: Transform programs into continuation-passing style (CPS); implement a CPS interpreter; describe continuation-based control operators (call/cc, shift/reset).
learning_plan.resources: Appel – Compiling with Continuations Ch. 1–2; Danvy & Filinski

learning_plan.llo: Describe ML-style module systems with signatures and functors; introduce dependent types and their role in verified programming (Coq/Agda overview).
learning_plan.resources: Pierce – TAPL Ch. 24; Coq Reference Manual (intro)

learning_plan.llo: Demonstrate a working interpreter or type checker for a small programming language incorporating formal semantic features from the course.

courses.desc: Advanced study of computational complexity; time and space complexity classes; P, NP, PSPACE, and the polynomial hierarchy; completeness, hardness, and reductions; randomized and approximation algorithms; lower bound techniques.

clos.description: Explain fundamental concepts of computational complexity including time and space complexity measures and the Church–Turing thesis.
Classify computational problems within the complexity hierarchy (P, NP, coNP, PSPACE, EXP) and explain their relationships.
Apply polynomial-time reductions to prove NP-hardness and NP-completeness of decision problems.
Analyze randomized complexity classes (RP, BPP, ZPP) and circuit complexity models.
Evaluate the implications of complexity theory for algorithm design, cryptography, and the P vs. NP open problem.

learning_plan.llo: Review deterministic and nondeterministic Turing machines, decidability, and the Church–Turing thesis as foundations for complexity.
Define time complexity classes P and NP; analyze the running times of algorithms and verify NP membership via polynomial verifiers.
Prove the Cook–Levin theorem establishing SAT as NP-complete; define polynomial-time many-one reducibility.
Prove NP-completeness of 3SAT, Vertex Cover, Clique, Hamiltonian Path, and Subset Sum via reductions.

learning_plan.topic: Space Complexity: PSPACE and Savitch's Theorem
learning_plan.llo: Define PSPACE and NPSPACE; prove Savitch's theorem; identify PSPACE-complete problems (TQBF).
Define the polynomial hierarchy (PH) using oracle machines and alternation; locate standard problems within PH.

learning_plan.topic: L and NL: Logarithmic Space Complexity
learning_plan.llo: Define L and NL; prove NL=coNL (Immerman–Szelepcsényi); solve NL-completeness problems (PATH).

learning_plan.topic: Randomized Complexity: RP, coRP, BPP, ZPP
learning_plan.llo: Define probabilistic Turing machines and randomized complexity classes; prove BPP ⊆ PH.
Analyze Boolean circuits, circuit families, and complexity classes NC and AC; discuss connections to parallel computation.
Define interactive proof systems and Arthur-Merlin games; understand the proof that IP = PSPACE.
learning_plan.resources: Arora & Barak Ch. 8; Shamir's IP=PSPACE paper

learning_plan.llo: Design approximation algorithms for NP-hard optimization problems; prove inapproximability results using PCP theorem.

learning_plan.topic: Cryptographic Complexity: One-Way Functions and Pseudorandomness
learning_plan.llo: Connect complexity assumptions (P≠NP) to cryptographic hardness; define one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.
learning_plan.resources: Arora & Barak Ch. 9; Goldreich Vol. I

learning_plan.topic: Open Problems, Barriers, and P vs. NP
learning_plan.llo: Discuss oracle relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization barriers; reflect on the P vs. NP problem and its significance.
learning_plan.resources: Aaronson's 'Why Philosophers Should Care About Computational Complexity'; Arora & Barak Ch. 3

Analyze randomized and circuit complexity through problem sets

courses.title: Advanced Operating Systems
courses.desc: Advanced concepts in operating system design and implementation; process and thread management, advanced scheduling algorithms, memory management, file systems, distributed OS concepts, virtualization, and security mechanisms in modern operating systems.

clos.description: Explain advanced OS design principles including kernel architectures, scheduling algorithms, and synchronization mechanisms.
Analyze virtual memory systems including paging, segmentation, TLBs, and page replacement policies.
Design and evaluate solutions to classical synchronization problems using semaphores, monitors, and lock-free techniques.
Assess file system design, storage management (RAID, SSDs), and I/O subsystems in modern operating systems.
Examine virtualization, containerization, and OS-level security mechanisms and their design trade-offs.

learning_plan.topic: OS Design Principles and Kernel Architectures
learning_plan.llo: Compare monolithic, microkernel, hybrid, and exokernel architectures; analyze the design trade-offs of each in terms of performance, modularity, and security.
Contrast kernel-level and user-level threads; analyze the Linux process model (fork, exec, clone); examine lightweight process implementations.
Analyze scheduling objectives and evaluate algorithms: CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler), real-time scheduling (EDF, RMS), and multiprocessor scheduling.
Implement solutions to mutual exclusion, producer-consumer, readers-writers, and dining philosophers problems using semaphores and monitors.
Model deadlock using resource-allocation graphs; implement Banker's algorithm; compare deadlock prevention, avoidance, and detection strategies.

learning_plan.topic: Virtual Memory: Paging, TLBs, and Page Tables
learning_plan.llo: Explain paging hardware, multi-level page tables, and TLB management; analyze address translation costs and TLB miss handling.

learning_plan.topic: Midterm Exam + Page Replacement and Memory Allocation
learning_plan.llo: Evaluate page replacement algorithms (FIFO, LRU, Clock, Working Set); analyze thrashing and working-set model; implement a memory allocator.
Explain file system structure, directory organization, and allocation methods (contiguous, linked, indexed); analyze ext4, NTFS, and ZFS designs.
Describe I/O hardware, polling vs. interrupt-driven I/O, and DMA; analyze device driver architecture in Linux.

learning_plan.topic: Storage Systems: RAID, SSDs, and Distributed Storage
learning_plan.llo: Analyze RAID levels and their trade-offs; compare HDD vs. SSD I/O models; examine distributed file systems (NFS, HDFS).
Distinguish Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors; explain hardware-assisted virtualization (VT-x); compare containers (Docker, LXC) with VMs.
learning_plan.resources: Silberschatz Ch. 18; Docker documentation; KVM documentation

learning_plan.topic: OS Security: Access Control and Security Modules
learning_plan.llo: Analyze access control models (DAC, MAC, RBAC); examine Linux Security Modules (SELinux, AppArmor); discuss common OS vulnerabilities.

learning_plan.topic: Distributed OS Concepts: Consistency and Fault Tolerance
learning_plan.llo: Explain distributed synchronization (logical clocks, vector clocks); analyze consistency models and fault-tolerance strategies in distributed systems.

learning_plan.topic: Case Studies: Linux, Windows, and macOS Internals
learning_plan.llo: Compare OS internals across Linux, Windows NT, and macOS/XNU; analyze key architectural decisions and their real-world implications.

assessment_blueprint.description: Explain OS design, scheduling, and process management through quizzes and problem sets
Analyze virtual memory and paging through the midterm exam
Design synchronization solutions in a programming assignment
Assess file and storage systems through problem sets
Examine virtualization and OS security through a lab and the final exam

courses.title: Special Topics in Computer Science
courses.desc: Advanced study of emerging and specialized topics in computer science not covered in regular courses. Topics vary by semester and reflect current developments and research trends in the field.

clos.description: Analyze recent advances and foundational concepts in the selected special topic area of computer science.
Evaluate methodologies, algorithms, and techniques used in current research literature on the special topic.
Apply techniques from the special topic to investigate or solve a focused computing problem through a project or paper.
Communicate research findings and critical analysis through written reports and oral presentations.

learning_plan.topic: Introduction: Scope, Motivation, and Overview of the Special Topic
learning_plan.llo: Describe the scope and significance of the special topic; identify key problems, applications, and open questions in the area.
Review foundational concepts and prerequisite knowledge necessary for understanding the special topic.
Explain and apply the primary concepts, models, or algorithms that define the special topic area.
Extend understanding of the topic's methods; apply techniques to worked examples or case studies.
Demonstrate current understanding through a midterm assessment; begin a systematic survey of the research literature.
learning_plan.methods: Midterm Exam; Lecture on literature review methodology

learning_plan.llo: Analyze advanced techniques and current state-of-the-art approaches from recent publications in the topic area.
Examine real-world applications of the special topic; critically evaluate the impact and limitations of existing solutions.

learning_plan.topic: Research Methodology for the Topic Area
learning_plan.llo: Identify appropriate research methods (empirical, theoretical, design science) for investigations in the special topic; formulate a research question.
Present progress on the term project; receive and incorporate peer and instructor feedback.
Present completed or near-complete project findings; demonstrate application of the special topic concepts.

learning_plan.topic: Final Paper Submission and Course Synthesis
learning_plan.llo: Submit a final written report; synthesize key insights from the course and reflect on open problems and future directions.

assessment_blueprint.description: Analyze foundational and core concepts through reading responses and the midterm assessment
Evaluate research literature through a paper critique and problem sets or labs
Apply special topic techniques in a focused project
Communicate findings through two oral presentations and a final written paper

courses.title: Special Project
courses.desc: An individual or group project requiring the application of computer science principles to a significant problem. Students design, implement, and evaluate a computing artifact or conduct a focused research investigation under faculty supervision.

clos.description: Identify and define a significant computing problem suitable for investigation through a special project.
Design a systematic project plan including objectives, methodology, timeline, and deliverables.
Implement and rigorously evaluate the proposed computing solution or research investigation.
Communicate project findings through technical documentation, a written report, and an oral defense.

learning_plan.topic: Project Orientation: Expectations, Requirements, and Ethics
learning_plan.llo: Understand the scope, deliverables, and ethical obligations of the special project; identify potential topic areas and supervisors.
Identify candidate project topics; assess technical feasibility, scope, and resource requirements through a preliminary investigation.
learning_plan.resources: ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, advisor guidance

learning_plan.llo: Conduct a focused review of relevant prior work; identify research gaps and the contribution of the proposed project.
Formulate a precise problem statement, research questions, and project objectives; define the scope and limitations.
Submit a complete project proposal covering problem statement, objectives, methodology, timeline, and expected outputs; present to advisor for feedback.

learning_plan.topic: Design Phase: Architecture, Methodology, and Tools
learning_plan.llo: Develop the detailed design of the project artifact or research methodology; select appropriate tools, frameworks, and evaluation criteria.
Present a progress report demonstrating partial implementation or preliminary results; identify blockers and adjust the project plan if needed.
Execute the first major phase of the project implementation or investigation; conduct iterative testing or data collection.

learning_plan.topic: Implementation / Investigation Phase II: Testing and Evaluation
learning_plan.llo: Complete implementation or data collection; conduct systematic evaluation using defined metrics, benchmarks, or experimental protocols.

learning_plan.topic: Analysis of Results and Iterative Refinement
learning_plan.llo: Analyze and interpret project results in relation to the research questions; refine the implementation or methodology based on findings.
Write a complete technical project report following academic writing conventions; produce user or system documentation for the project artifact.
Deliver a formal oral presentation and defense of the project; respond to questions from the panel; submit the final report and all project artifacts.

assessment_blueprint.tool: Topic Brief + Literature Review + Problem Statement

assessment_blueprint.description: Design the project through the proposal and design document

Communicate findings through the final report and oral defense
